# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to permanently face its star. This phenomenon, common among exoplanets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the stark temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, under perpetual stellar bombardment, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock, while the nightside plummets to hundreds of degrees below zero. Without atmospheric redistribution, this divide would render both sides potentially uninhabitable.

However, atmospheres and oceans serve as powerful climate equalizers. Winds transport heat from the dayside toward the nightside, while ocean currents perform similar work. On planets with thick atmospheres, like modeled "eyeball Earths," this circulation can maintain a temperate region at the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night—where liquid water might persist. Some models suggest such planets could remain habitable even at the outer edges of red dwarf habitable zones.

Tidal locking also influences atmospheric escape. Because many tidally locked planets orbit close to their stars, they face intense stellar radiation and winds that can strip atmospheres entirely. A robust magnetic field and sufficient atmospheric mass become critical for climate preservation. Interestingly, some research suggests that a thick dayside atmosphere can actually protect against this erosion.
